records.author: UN Secretary-General
records.title: Human rights in the administration of justice: report of the Secretary-General
records.short_title: Secretary-General's report on human rights in the administration of justice

passages.text: The present report is submitted pursuant to General Assembly resolution 79/172. It builds on the prior thematic report submitted by the Secretary-General to the General Assembly at its seventy-ninth session and on other reports and resolutions. The report draws on information received from Member States, United Nations entities, human rights mechanisms and civil society and on external research.

Neurotechnology has advanced rapidly since the Secretary-General first referred to it in his report entitled “Our Common Agenda” as a frontier issue requiring the clarification of applicable human rights frameworks and standards (see A/75/982). Devices that were until recently confined to clinical or research environments are now entering, or may enter, consumer markets, workplaces, schools, public services, law enforcement and justice systems. The convergence of neurotechnology with artificial intelligence is expanding the capacity to process and interpret neural data and to derive increasingly complex inferences from it.

These developments hold significant promise, particularly for medical and assistive applications. Neurotechnology has already delivered major benefits in healthcare, notably in neurorehabilitation, where brain-computer interfaces aid movement, communication and recovery. However, the developments also raise profound questions for the protection of human rights, especially in the administration of justice. When applied in the administration of justice, these technologies serve different purposes and pose distinct legal and human rights risks, especially as tools and data developed for medical use are repurposed without appropriate safeguards being in place.

passages.section: and other emerging technologies A. Neurotechnology and neural data
passages.text: For the purposes of the present report, neurotechnology is understood as “devices, systems and procedures – encompassing both hardware and software – that directly measure, access, monitor, analyse, predict or modulate the nervous system to understand, influence, restore or anticipate its structure, activity and function”. Neurotechnologies may be invasive or non-invasive: non-invasive techniques, such as electroencephalography, rely on external sensors, whereas invasive technologies involve the surgical implantation of electrodes or other devices. They serve two principal functions. The first is to measure and analyse nervous system activity such as: electroencephalographs used to record the brain’s electrical activity; functional magnetic resonance imaging, a form of neuroimaging used to measure brain activity by detecting changes in blood flow; and brain-computer interfaces, used to translate brain signals into commands for devices. The second function is to intervene in or modulate neural activity through neuromodulation, such as deep brain stimulation. Invasive neurotechnologies generally must be licensed medical devices, and the data that they gather are generally protected under national health data privacy laws. Non-invasive neurotechnologies used in general consumer markets are generally subject to little or no regulation, even though wearable devices are also medicalgrade, and the data that they collect are extremely sensitive.

passages.section: and other emerging technologies A. Neurotechnology and neural data
passages.text: The operation of neurotechnology can generate neural data, defined as “qualitative and quantitative data about the structure, activity and function of the nervous system gathered through neurotechnology”. There is broad consensus that neural data are highly sensitive, providing unprecedented access to internal mental states, and that they require heightened ethical and legal protection.

passages.section: Neuroimaging as medical or expert evidence
passages.text: At present, the most common use of neurotechnology in judicial contexts is the introduction of neuroimaging as medical or expert evidence. In criminal proceedings, neuroimaging is most frequently presented to support mitigation claims at sentencing, and to corroborate claims of psychosocial disability or claims related to capacity. Where accepted, such material is generally treated as corroborative rather than determinative. In civil proceedings, neuroimaging is used to assess non-pecuniary damages, corroborate claims of chronic pain or cognitive impairment, and in the examination of legal capacity.

passages.section: Neuroimaging as medical or expert evidence
passages.text: While the admissibility and evidentiary weight of neuroimaging remain contested, several jurisdictions permit its limited and carefully circumscribed use: in Brazil, it remains largely confined to clinical mental health expertise; in at least two decisions in the Kingdom of the Netherlands, courts of appeal have accepted neuroimaging and neuropsychological evidence as corroborative material; in the United States of America, since an early case in 1992, criminal defendants have been increasingly introducing neurobiological evidence to challenge their own competency and the effectiveness of defence counsel at trial, and to mitigate punishment; at least two decisions in Italian courts have relied on neuroimaging including at the appellate stage; in at least two cases, the Court of Appeal of England and Wales has accepted neuroscientific evidence as corroborative – using it to support rather than determine assessments of culpability and sentencing: and in Canada, neuroscientific evidence has been used in both criminal and civil proceedings, including in end-of-life decision-making, but is not treated as determinative.

Less commonly, neurotechnology has been used in interrogation contexts, especially for brain-based deception detection. This is an umbrella term for technologies that measure central nervous system activity with the goal of “detecting deception”. From the neural data retrieved, probabilistic inferences are drawn about certain mental states and about cognitive processes, like memory or recognition of a place. The most discussed application is the use of functional magnetic resonance imaging for “lie detection”. Other related but distinct techniques are “guilty knowledge” or “concealed information” testing, which are commercialized under labels such as “brain fingerprinting” and brain electrical oscillation signature profiling. These techniques measure physiological or brain responses to determine whether a person recognizes concealed or crime-related information.

These brain-based deception detection techniques raise serious concerns regarding consent, coercion, reliability, and the privilege against self-incrimination. No brain-based deception detection method has achieved general acceptance for courtroom use. A United States federal appeals court excluded lie detection evidence based on functional magnetic resonance imaging, finding it insufficiently reliable and not generally accepted under evidentiary standards. The Supreme Court of India held that the involuntary administration of brain electrical oscillation signature profiling tests violates the constitutional protection against self-incrimination and renders the resulting evidence inadmissible. However, voluntary use appears to have continued in practice.

Looking ahead, potential applications of neurotechnology in the administration of justice are increasingly discussed, although most applications remain experimental. Some research claims that certain neurotechnologies can assess the risk of recidivism and, when combined with artificial intelligence, could produce individualized psychological profiles based on neural markers, that could be used to predict behaviour. The prospect of identifying individuals as future offenders before an offence has been committed raises particularly serious human rights concerns, including related to the presumption of innocence.

Neurotechnology is also likely to be explored for use in interrogations through the process of “decoding”, in which artificial-intelligence algorithms attempt to translate brain signals into readable information about thoughts, intentions or memories. Whether such approaches will, at some point, be able to produce information that is sufficiently reliable to be used in the administration of justice is unknown. If they were able to be deployed, they would likely have an impact on a range of human rights, including privacy and freedom of thought.

Other anticipated developments include the use of wearable neurotechnology, including for the surveillance and monitoring of offenders outside custodial settings. This application would significantly expand State oversight of individuals’ inner lives. There is also research on the use of neurostimulation to modulate neural processes associated with aggression or impulse control. Both of these technologies, if ever considered for use in the administration of justice, would likely raise complex human rights issues that should be addressed before the technologies are deployed.

A key concern regarding the use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice is the reliability of neuroscientific evidence in court. While such technologies produce detailed data, their accurate application in legal settings remains challenging. Brain data are complex and uncertain, and links between brain activity and behaviour can be misunderstood, potentially leading to incorrect conclusions about an individual’s mental state. Particular caution is warranted when translating findings established at the group or population level into conclusions about individual persons, given intra- and inter-individual variability and the probabilistic nature of many neuroscientific findings. Problems are worsened by the gap between controlled laboratory conditions and real-world settings, and by the lack of a shared understanding between lawyers and scientists, which makes it difficult for courts to assess the probative value of such evidence.

A further concern is that, as neurotechnology becomes increasingly commercialized, large volumes of neural data are reportedly being collected by consumer technology companies. Wearable electroencephalography devices, marketed for wellness, gaming or productivity, are widely available. Such consumer data may reportedly be accessed by State authorities or introduced as evidence in legal proceedings without recognition of its uniquely sensitive character, a risk amplified in counter-terrorism and national security contexts, where legal thresholds for data access and admissibility are often significantly lower.

passages.section: III. Legal framework and State obligations
passages.text: The human rights framework governing the administration of justice includes the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Neurotechnology use in justice may engage rights to freedom from torture and ill-treatment, liberty and security of person, equality before courts, a fair trial, privacy, freedom of thought, expression and opinion, non-discrimination and an effective remedy. Other relevant treaties include the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

passages.section: III. Legal framework and State obligations
passages.text: The Secretary-General and the Human Rights Council have emphasized that the use of technology by Member States must be consistent with international human rights standards. The Human Rights Committee has clarified that States Parties to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights should put in place a framework that prevents human rights violations, holds those responsible to account and provides remedies, in relation to both the actions and the omissions of States. Under the principle of due diligence, States Parties are required to take measures to protect individuals from harm by third parties, including business enterprises. Business enterprises, in turn, have responsibilities regarding respect for human rights, which should guide the design, development and deployment of neurotechnology, in accordance with the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (A/HRC/17/31, annex). While some contend that the challenges of neurotechnology may require development of new legal frameworks, others affirm that the risks of misuse or abuse of neurotechnology may be addressed within the existing international human rights law framework, including through potential further interpretations and clarifications that might be undertaken by United Nations human rights mechanisms.

passages.section: IV. Impact of neurotechnology on human rights
passages.text: Neurotechnology and the processing of neural data have been addressed by a growing number of United Nations resolutions and reports underscoring their relevance, associated risks, and the need for regulatory frameworks to protect human rights. The potential for misuse of neurotechnology to result in large-scale human rights violations is an increasing concern.

Neurotechnology accesses, measures and analyses brain signals. If these signals are treated as direct indicators of thoughts, intentions or truthfulness, the use of neural data points could undermine how we understand and value each of us as human beings. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights affirms that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights and are endowed with reason and conscience. Many treaties give expression to dignity in particular settings, and article 3 of the Universal Declaration on Bioethics and Human Rights of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) affirms that the interests and welfare of the individual should have priority over the sole interest of science or society.

In the context of neurotechnology, the Special Rapporteur on the right to privacy identifies human dignity as a fundamental guiding principle for the regulation of neurotechnology (see A/HRC/58/58). UNESCO also identifies human dignity as a cardinal value guiding the whole life cycle of neurotechnology. According to research, dignity logically requires that persons be treated as autonomous subjects rather than as biological objects to be decoded or manipulated. At the same time, dignity is enhanced when for example neurotechnology is used to restore autonomy and inclusion, such as when assistive brain-computer interfaces enable persons with significant physical impairments to communicate or move.

passages.section: B. Freedom of thought and opinion
passages.text: Neurotechnologies used to infer mental states, memory or recognition, through brain-based deception detection technology or decoding, could reveal information that the person has not chosen to disclose. Coercive neuromodulation technologies can alter brain activity and shape how thoughts occur. Such technologies could thus have a profound impact on the freedom of thought, recognized in article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The Human Rights Committee has affirmed that the freedom of thought, conscience and religion is “far-reaching and profound; it encompasses freedom of thought on all matters”, and that the freedom of thought and conscience “does not permit any limitations”. The fundamental character of the right is reflected in the fact that derogation from article 18 is prohibited, even in time of public emergency, and the Committee has considered that States may not make reservations to this provision.

passages.section: B. Freedom of thought and opinion
passages.text: The Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief stated that “despite its proclaimed importance and absolute nature”, the scope and content of the right to freedom of thought “remain largely underdeveloped and poorly understood” (A/76/380, para. 4). Experts emphasize the urgent need to address this gap, particularly given neurotechnologies’ potential to access mental content and influence cognition, emotion, and behaviour. Acts that seek to alter thoughts, such as “ideology conversion” programmes, may violate the right to freedom of thought and opinion, and “no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts”. The main element of the right to freedom of thought and conscience has been identified as the right of everyone to develop thoughts and conscience autonomously, free from impermissible external interference or alteration. Experts have argued that four pillars of freedom of thought are most relevant to neurotechnology: the freedom not to disclose thoughts; freedom from punishment for thoughts, real or inferred; freedom from impermissible alteration of thoughts; and an enabling environment for free thought.

passages.section: B. Freedom of thought and opinion
passages.text: Neurotechnology may potentially affect all four pillars of freedom of thought. Neurotechnologies capable of inferring mental states and revealing information that the person has not chosen to disclose may impact the freedom not to disclose thoughts. While neurotechnology is not capable at present of “mind-reading”, it is reportedly capable of inferring emotions and internal reactions based on neural data (see A/HRC/57/61). The freedom from punishment for thoughts could be threatened should such inference result in sanctions. Individuals have an unlimited right to think whatever they wish, whether in terms of actual thoughts or inferred ones (see A/76/380). The freedom from impermissible alteration of thoughts could be impacted by coercive neuromodulation, which may alter or shape a person’s thoughts.

passages.section: B. Freedom of thought and opinion
passages.text: Freedom of thought contributes to freedom of opinion in that opinions usually represent the result of a thought process. Given the overlapping nature of these freedoms, representing part of the “forum internum”, neurotechnology presents similar risks to freedom of opinion as to thought. Article 19 (1) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights protects the right to have and form opinions without interference. According to the Human Rights Committee, this right is one to which the Covenant permits no exception or restriction, and protects all forms of opinion, including political, scientific, historical, moral and religious opinions. Harassment, intimidation or stigmatization of a person on account of opinions held is forbidden. Forced neurological interventions, indoctrination programmes or threats of violence designed to compel individuals to form particular opinions or change their opinion would violate this freedom (see A/73/348). The Constitutional Court of Spain decided that “ideological freedom” is a combination of the freedoms of thought and opinion, protecting the mind from technologies capable of modulating or manipulating political beliefs.

Neurotechnologies can access the brain to collect and record highly sensitive information and affect physical and mental privacy by exposing the individual’s private space and integrity. Articles 17 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and article 16 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child protect individuals from arbitrary or unlawful interference with their privacy. Neurotechnology introduces new threats to privacy by significantly increasing the level of possible interference. According to the Human Rights Committee, if an interference is unlawful, or arbitrary – interpreted broadly to include elements of inappropriateness, injustice, lack of predictability and due process of law, as well as elements of reasonableness, necessity and proportionality – it could amount to a violation of the right to privacy.

As emphasized by the Human Rights Committee, the right to privacy protects personal data, communications and the integrity of private life. This protection would include neural data. Neural data are uniquely revealing since they are capable of disclosing certain aspects of identity and personality. Consumer neurotechnology companies already collect unknown quantities of users’ personal data, with the expectation that such data will become more decipherable in the future. Neural data is biometric in character and may reportedly be re-identified across data sets and yield insights that were not foreseeable at the time of collection. According to research, it is also reportedly often unclear to consumers whether or how their data can be deleted once collected.

For the purposes of protecting the right to privacy, the Human Rights Committee has emphasized that: the gathering and holding of personal information must be regulated by law; that effective measures must ensure that such information does not reach unauthorized persons; and that every individual must be able to ascertain whether, and if so what, personal data is stored, for what purposes and by whom, and to seek rectification or elimination of incorrect data. These requirements would also apply to neural data and other information retrieved through the use of neurotechnologies.

The Special Rapporteur on the right to privacy has set out, in detail, the foundations and principles for the regulation of neurotechnology and the processing of neural data, including the protection of human dignity and mental privacy. The Rapporteur also detailed a framework for national enforcement through a model law (see A/80/283).

The prohibition of torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment is absolute and non-derogable and extends not only to physical pain but also to acts that cause mental suffering. Persons in detention also have the right to be “treated with humanity and with respect for the inherent dignity of the human person”. The use of brain-based lie detection, decoding of readable information about thoughts, intentions or memories, coercive interrogation techniques, and neuromodulation, applied in detention or investigative contexts, may result in mental or physical suffering contravening the protection provided under articles 7 and 10 (1) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

The Human Rights Council Advisory Committee is of the view that the use of neuromodulation techniques intended to alter the brain activity of offenders to reduce aggression or impulsivity may constitute treatment contrary to articles 7 or 10 of the Covenant when imposed without genuinely free and informed consent (see A/HRC/57/61). In custodial settings, the pronounced power imbalance between the State and the individual may call into question the genuineness of consent. Experts affirm that where such techniques are presented in connection with prospects such as early release or favourable parole outcomes, there is a significant risk that consent may not be fully free or voluntary. Article 7 of the Covenant “expressly prohibits medical or scientific experimentation without the free consent of the person concerned”. The difficulty of establishing that consent is genuinely free given the particularly vulnerable status of those who are detained has been acknowledged by the Human Rights Committee.

The application of neurotechnology in places of detention, from passive cognitive surveillance to neuromodulation, would pose unique challenges to the right under article 10 (1) of the Covenant of all those deprived of their liberty to be treated with humanity and dignity. “Humanity” means that detainees should not be subjected to any hardship or constraint other than that resulting from the deprivation of liberty itself. Constant monitoring of the brains of those detained as a form of surveillance could cause mental distress.

passages.section: E. Judicial independence and fair trial
passages.text: The introduction of neurotechnology, particularly in combination with artificial intelligence, poses significant risks to judicial independence, protected under article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. This article stipulates that everyone is entitled to a fair and public hearing by a competent, independent and impartial tribunal established by law. When the design, implementation and oversight of artificial intelligence-enhanced tools are the responsibility of the executive branch alone, or when such systems are outsourced to private companies whose proprietary models are shielded by intellectual property safeguards, the independence of the judiciary may be jeopardized. The phenomenon of automation bias – the tendency to accept uncritically the outputs of technological systems – can represent a further threat to independent judicial reasoning.

passages.section: E. Judicial independence and fair trial
passages.text: The right to a fair trial is engaged in multiple ways by the use of neurotechnology. The coercive use of brain-based lie detection could call into question the privilege against self-incrimination, protected under article 14 (3) (g) of the Covenant. This privilege is an absolute guarantee and any direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure on the accused with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt is prohibited. The Supreme Court of India, in Selvi v. State of Karnataka, held that the involuntary administration of brain electrical oscillation signature profiling tests, a form of brain-based lie detection, violates the constitutional protection against self-incrimination. In addition, under the exclusionary rule, statements or other evidence obtained in violation of the prohibition of torture or ill-treatment may not be invoked as evidence in any proceedings. This could apply to evidence obtained through the coercive use of neurotechnologies.

passages.section: E. Judicial independence and fair trial
passages.text: Beyond the privilege against self-incrimination, the use of predictive neurotechnology purporting to assess future criminality may also undermine the presumption of innocence. Neurotechnology may also pose substantial challenges to the principle of equality of arms, which would require the defence to have access to the scientific expertise and proprietary data needed to interpret and challenge neurotechnology-derived evidence. According to submissions and research, the right to a fair trial also depends on requiring that any neurotechnology-based evidence admitted in court meets the highest standards of scientific validation, transparency and contestability.

Neurotechnologies claiming to assess the risk of recidivism, and the use of brain-based deception technologies to determine whether a person should be detained, may lead to arbitrary detention under article 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. This right protects liberty of person, meaning freedom from confinement of the body, and security of person, meaning freedom from injury to the body and the mind. Bodily and mental integrity is also protected by article 7 of the Covenant. The prohibition of arbitrary detention under article 9 means that the decision to detain, or continue to detain, a person must be based on reasons specific to that individual. Neurotechnologies used for risk assessments often rely on statistical correlations from non-representative data sets, potentially leading to prolonged or preventive detention based on what a person might do rather than what the person has done. Detention based on neural data may also be considered arbitrary, when the right to challenge confinement is undermined by the untransparent and obscure nature of such systems – sometimes referred to as a “black box” – making it difficult for legal professionals or the accused to understand the rationale behind detention decisions (see A/79/296).

passages.section: G. Equality before the law and recognition as a person before the law
passages.text: Neurotechnology claiming to assess the potential for recidivism risks prioritizing biological determinism over recognition of the individual as a legal subject. Several human rights treaties protect the right to recognition as a person before the law. This means that every human being must be acknowledged as a “legal person” everywhere, with the capacity to hold rights and duties under the law. They must be treated as subjects rather than objects of the law, something that could be undermined by such use of neurotechnology. Use of coercive neuromodulation that alters personality, affective responses or cognitive recall could also constitute a direct threat to the right to recognition as a person before the law. At the same time, neurotechnology can be used to enable people to exercise and claim their rights, as assistive brain-computer interfaces allow persons with certain disabilities to express their will and preferences, thereby supporting legal agency.

passages.section: H. Right to an effective remedy and accountability
passages.text: The opaque nature of many neurotechnological and algorithmic systems may frustrate the right to an effective remedy, protected under article 2 (3) of the Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, by making it difficult for people to understand or contest the rationale behind decisions that may affect their liberty or other human rights. The unique challenges posed by neurotechnology may mean that affected persons may not even become aware that a violation has occurred, potentially rendering the right to a remedy “illusory, inaccessible or ineffective” and raising accountability issues (A/HRC/57/61, para. 72).

The Human Rights Council Advisory Committee has identified “groups experiencing structural discrimination and marginalized people or those in positions of socioeconomic disadvantage” as being particularly vulnerable to negative impacts of the use of neurotechnology in the administration of justice (A/HRC/57/61, para. 37). Addressing these risks requires specific legislative and policy responses. Discrimination stems from biased training data, tools validated on limited populations and structural inequalities in criminal justice systems. These technologies may disproportionately affect women by reinforcing gender stereotypes and institutional biases, as they often rely on non-representative, male-centric data sets that can distort assessments of veracity or recidivism risk.

Neurotechnology may affect Indigenous Peoples collectively, having an impact beyond an individual rights framework. Protection should therefore recognize their rights to self-determination, cultural heritage and traditional knowledge under the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The collection, storage, processing and sharing of neural data of Indigenous Peoples may raise concerns similar to those relating to genetic resources and digital data and should be governed in accordance with Indigenous Peoples’ rights to own and control such data and to consent to and benefit from their use, which includes protection against misuse and exploitation by States or business enterprises (see A/HRC/60/66).

Technology is never neutral, but reflects the values and interests of those who influence its design and use, and is fundamentally shaped by the same structures of inequality that operate in society (see A/HRC/44/57). People of African descent and racialized minorities are disproportionately affected by algorithmic bias in data sets that underrepresent them and by predictive tools that mirror and amplify historical discrimination. Indigenous Peoples, minorities and people of African descent may also be disproportionately exposed to the deployment of neurotechnology, given their disproportionate representation in criminal justice systems (see A/HRC/60/75). Inclusive validation, cultural competence, community-based governance, accountability and the meaningful participation of affected groups are essential preconditions for the lawful deployment of neurotechnology, including in the administration of justice.

Children’s heightened brain plasticity makes them especially vulnerable to coercive alteration and to permanent labelling on the basis of predictive risk assessments before their personalities are fully formed. States are urged to identify, define and prohibit digital practices that manipulate or interfere with children’s freedom of thought, in the administration of justice.

While neurotechnology can enable accessibility communication and inclusion when developed in partnership with organizations representing persons with disabilities and is based on free and informed consent, persons with disabilities and neurodivergent individuals may experience misinterpretation of atypical neural patterns, pressure towards forced “normalization” and discrimination on the basis of neurological difference.

passages.section: V. National and regional regulation and emerging guidelines
passages.text: At the national level, the regulatory response to the human rights challenges posed by neurotechnology is still nascent and uneven (see A/HRC/57/61).

passages.section: V. National and regional regulation and emerging guidelines
passages.text: In Chile, in 2023, the Supreme Court applied the 2021 constitutional amendment, to protect brain activity and derived data, holding unlawful a company’s practices involving a portable brain-monitoring device. The ruling was among the first globally to address neural data under the rights to mental privacy and physical and mental integrity. In Mexico, a proposed general law on neurorights and neurotechnologies would establish a national commission of neuroethics and neurolaw. In Brazil, neural data is classified as sensitive personal data, and Rio Grande do Sul has enshrined “neurorights” protections in its state constitution.

passages.section: V. National and regional regulation and emerging guidelines
passages.text: In the European Union, under the Artificial Intelligence Act of 2024, artificial intelligence-driven neurotechnologies and emotion-recognition systems may be classified as high-risk where they involve profiling or affect fundamental rights and they are subject to strict compliance requirements. The León Declaration on European Neurotechnology, signed by European Union ministers in 2023, affirms a humancentred and rights-based approach. In France, a law on bioethics adopted in 2021 permits decrees banning activities that modify cerebral activity and present a serious or suspected health risk. In Spain, the non-binding Charter of Digital Rights, adopted in 2021, addresses neurotechnology and mental privacy, while submissions received from Austria, Italy, Slovenia and Ukraine described adaptations of data protection and bioethics frameworks.

passages.section: V. National and regional regulation and emerging guidelines
passages.text: In 2024, China adopted ethical guidelines for brain-computer interface research covering research integrity, scientific validity and informed consent. While the United States has no federal neurotechnology-specific laws, California, Colorado and Montana have extended sensitive data protections to neural data, and the American Medical Association has defined neural data as information obtained through neurotechnology. Submissions received from Morocco and Uzbekistan describe ongoing legislative and policy efforts on neurotechnology within the broader context of data protection and digital health reforms.

passages.section: V. National and regional regulation and emerging guidelines
passages.text: The Inter-American Declaration of Principles regarding Neuroscience, Neurotechnologies and Human Rights of 2023 adopts a human rights-based approach. At the international level, the General Conference of UNESCO adopted its Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology in 2025, which calls for national coordinating bodies for neurotechnology, among other measures. In 2019, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development adopted a recommendation on responsible innovation in neurotechnology containing nine guiding principles, such as the safeguarding of personal brain data. The Human Rights Council has tasked its Advisory Committee with drafting guidelines on applying existing human rights standards throughout the neurotechnology life cycle for consideration at its sixty-fourth session. In 2025, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the International Criminal Police Organization launched a collaboration to explore the potential uses of neurotechnology in law enforcement and criminal justice, and the associated risks.

Neurotechnology, including new and emerging forms, raises profound human rights challenges when applied to the administration of justice. Its expansion beyond clinical settings into investigative, judicial and correctional contexts introduces significant risks, alongside potential benefits. By enabling access to and possible interference with the brain, its use may affect a wide spectrum of human rights, including the rights to human dignity, privacy, freedom of thought, a fair trial, protection against self-incrimination and the presumption of innocence, as well as the prohibition of torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. At the same time, the evidentiary use of neuroscientific data remains contested. Its technical complexity, probabilistic nature and potential for misinterpretation pose significant risks, particularly in legal settings that lack a robust scientific or legal frameworks.

International human rights law provides an applicable framework to address the risks of neurotechnology, but further clarification and consistent application are needed. International human rights law mechanisms, including those of the United Nations human rights mechanisms, should, within the scope of their respective mandates, consider the implications of the use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice in order to provide guidance to States to ensure that their use of such technologies is aligned with their human rights obligations.

Neural data, as uniquely sensitive personal data, demand heightened protection, especially considering their increasing collection by private actors and potential reuse in legal proceedings. Current regulatory approaches remain fragmented and insufficient, underscoring the need for comprehensive, human rights-based governance.
I recommend that Member States:

Establish regulatory frameworks, consistent with international human rights law and relevant international standards and guidance provided by United Nations human rights mechanisms, governing the development, deployment and use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including their development by business enterprises or other entities. This could include mapping existing national frameworks applicable to neurotechnology in the administration of justice and adopting legislative and policy measures to address identified gaps. Regulation should require the conduct of human rights impact assessments and due diligence across the entire life cycle of neurotechnologies, including data-testing protocols and thresholds to identify and mitigate risks of algorithmic bias;

Recognize neural data as highly sensitive personal data subject to the highest level of legal protection; impose clear limitations on its collection, processing, sale, storage, retention, reuse and sharing; and provide accessible mechanisms for remedy in the event of infringement and effective judicial and independent oversight;

Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection, predictive applications, decoding applications to “read” thoughts, intentions or memories, neuromodulation and arbitrary or unlawful cognitive surveillance and monitoring;

Prohibit the use of neurotechnology as a means of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, or for any kind of social control or coercive behavioural conformity. Prohibit the use of neural data obtained through torture or ill-treatment, or in violation of the rights to freedom of thought and opinion, as evidence in any proceedings;

Require free, prior, informed, explicit and revocable consent for any potential use of neurotechnology in the administration of justice, accompanied by full transparency regarding risks, access to independent legal counsel of one’s own choice and effective avenues for redress. Given the constrained and coercive nature of justice settings, any consent should be subject to the highest evidentiary standards and rigorous scrutiny;

Require rigorous independent scientific review and validation of any neurotechnology-derived evidence proposed for admission in court, including assessment, as appropriate, of its safety, validity, reliability, reproducibility, known limitations and suitability for the specific context and population in which it is applied. Accompany any lawful deployment of neurotechnology in the administration of justice with effective oversight, accountability and governance mechanisms and incorporate continuous monitoring and evaluation, transparency and public reporting;

Ensure enhanced safeguards for children, detainees, persons with disabilities, women, older persons, persons belonging to particular racial or ethnic groups, including people of African descent, Indigenous Peoples and persons in situations of vulnerability, with particular attention to the conditions of consent and the potentially disproportionate or discriminatory impact of these technologies on specific groups. Consult with and actively involve all affected communities or groups with regard to policies on or the use of such technologies;

Ensure that the development and deployment of neurotechnology respects the rights of Indigenous Peoples, including the requirement of free, prior and informed consent, and the protection of their collective rights, cultural integrity and self-determination under the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples;

Urge all business enterprises involved in neurotechnology to take all steps to meet their responsibility to respect human rights through operationalization of the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, including through human rights due diligence, transparency, plain-language consumer information, safety-by-design approaches and access to effective remedy;

Invest in human rights-based public education in neurotechnology literacy, as well as specialized training for law enforcement officials, prosecutors, judges and defence counsel, including risk evaluation and responsible decisionmaking.

passages.text: Encompassing a range of technological innovations and devices, neurotechnologies measure, decode, and/or alter neural data, which is information obtained by measuring the activity of a person's central or peripheral nervous system. Neurotechnology tools and methods monitor, interpret, or influence brain activity, including through neuroimaging techniques, cognitive assessments, and transcranial stimulation. For example, brain–computer interfaces (BCIs), in combination with Artificial Intelligence (AI) decoding systems, are used to interpret brain signals to allow individuals with paralysis to control the movement of their limbs, advanced prosthetics, an exoskeleton, or a vehicle. They have also been used to decode human thought in the form of words into text on a screen. Wearable technologies also constitute a growing portion of the consumer technology market, with non-invasive BCIs promising a range of benefits including improved concentration, maximized sleep, optimized sporting performance, enhanced gaming, and open-source tools for researchers, developers, and hobbyists. It is important to note, however, that more invasive methods are also developing at a rapid pace.

Neurotechnology holds the potential to offer innovative solutions and deliver better preventive and therapeutic treatments, benefiting humanity as a whole and providing opportunities for health improvements around the world. Indeed, studies have shown that one in three people are affected by neurological conditions, making them the leading cause of illness and disability worldwide.

As these technologies advance in precision and accessibility, they are increasingly considered for use in criminal investigations for lie detection and risk assessments. The possible integration of advanced neurotechnologies into law enforcement would constitute a significant and complex development in contemporary legal practice. However, in the context of the criminal justice system, the use of brain scans is not an entirely new phenomenon and scans from the neurotechnologies found in hospitals have for some time been used in expert evidence in some jurisdictions to support claims related to legal insanity, risk, intent, culpability, and type of punishment.

These potential applications raise profound questions about the future role of science and technology in legal determinations and how standards of admissible evidence may evolve. The proposed use of neurotechnology in these domains additionally raises serious ethical and legal concerns. The protection of human rights – particularly privacy, autonomy, non-discrimination, and due process – are central to this complex and emerging global debate, and are related to issues surrounding the reliability of neuroscientific methods, the risk of over-reliance on expert testimony, and the prospect of accessing or interpreting an individual’s internal thoughts in the form of words and mental states.

At the same time, there are promising potential uses of emerging neurotechnologies for the reintegration of incarcerated persons back into society. For example, EEG neurofeedback headsets have been examined for their potential to train self-regulation abilities in offenders suffering from various disorders;non-invasive brain stimulation has been examined for its potential use in improving decisionmaking behaviours among violent offenders,and transcranial magnetic stimulation has been used to assist in the treatment of depression and OCD, among other conditions.

While these devices may present treatment opportunities for those facing mental health challenges – who are overrepresented in prison settings and for whom incarceration has exacerbated mental health issues – many of these studies are preliminary. Additionally, given the vulnerability of this population, the neurotechnologies used in this context must not be used to further discriminate against these individuals.

The international community has recognized the importance of leveraging technology as a global public good, while safeguarding against human rights risks. This objective on human rights-compliant neurotechnology was acknowledged by United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres in Our Common Agenda, where he said “consideration should, for instance, be given to updating or clarifying our application of human rights frameworks and standards to address frontier issues and prevent harms in the digital or technology spaces, including in relation to . . . neuro-technology.”

This commitment is also evident in the first United Nations General Assembly Resolution on Artificial Intelligence (AI), which promotes the use of AI to advance the globally agreed goals of the 2030 Agenda while safeguarding against AI use cases that intrude upon human rights. This need for the responsible use of technology is also acknowledged in other global political commitments that pertain specifically to the criminal justice sector, as elaborated in the Kyoto Declaration and in successive resolutions of the UN General Assembly and Human Rights Council. The commitment to the responsible use of AI extends towards law enforcement as well. In 2023, INTERPOL and UNICRI jointly launched a Toolkit for Responsible AI Innovation in Law Enforcement.

In the context of the global commitments undertaken by States, including States’ obligations under international human rights law, UNODC and INTERPOL have a pivotal role to play in facilitating global dialogue, and in guiding law enforcement agencies and criminal justice institutions toward a responsible stance with respect to emerging developments in neurotechnology and AI, while promoting human-rights-based approaches.

This background paper shares some preliminary thoughts on the field of neurotechnology and its significance for law enforcement and the criminal justice system, focusing on opportunities, risks, and human rights safeguards. The emerging use of neurotechnology in these fields highlights the importance of involving policing and justice sector professionals in the identification of regulatory gaps and emerging threats, including those that relate to the malicious and/or criminal misuse of these technologies. An important consideration is that there are currently few legal frameworks in place to criminalize the malicious or irresponsible use of neurotechnologies.

passages.section: II. Uses in Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice
passages.text: Neurotechnology offers a range of potential applications within law enforcement and the criminal justice system. These include supporting crime prevention, investigation, and prosecution, as well as post-release support. Potential uses include memory detection, risk assessment, the decoding of thoughts in the form of words, or neuroenhancement. Researchers are also examining the possible use of BCIs to monitor stress levels or emotional states of law enforcement personnel in the field, building on existing detection systems and potentially opening new avenues for operational support and officer well-being. It is important to note that these use cases vary significantly in their level of scientific validity and technical readiness, with many still in experimental or early deployment stages.

passages.section: II. Uses in Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice
passages.text: While the relationship between neurotechnology, law enforcement, and the justice system is complex, the growing intersection of neuroscience and policing presents significant opportunities. Realizing the potential benefits of these technologies will depend on frameworks that ensure rigorous regulation, enforceable accountability, and oversight. A demonstrable and significant benefit for law enforcement functions must also be shown, and the necessity and proportionality of their use assessed against the potential human rights impacts.

passages.section: A. Application in the context of Law Enforcement
passages.text: The application of neurotechnology in law enforcement presents a wide range of risks and challenges that must be carefully considered before adoption. Brain activity is among the most intimate forms of personal information, and any attempt to monitor, decode or manipulate it for identification, investigative, preventive or therapeutic purposes without genuine consent would represent a profound intrusion into human dignity, autonomy, and privacy. As noted in a report by the UN Special Rapporteur on the right to privacy, neurotechnologies present a range of risks, including those related to the improper processing of neural data in ways that are contrary to human dignity, the theft of information, and the tracking or manipulation of individuals’ mental experiences. To ensure compliance with international human rights law, law enforcement and criminal justice institutions will need to ensure individuals’ rights to privacy, freedom of thought, bodily integrity, non-discrimination, and the prohibition of torture, inhuman and degrading treatment. Due process rights are also at stake, including the right to appear before a competent judicial authority, the presumption of innocence, the privilege against self-incrimination, and the right to appeal. Additionally, there is concern about the potential for neurotechnology to be used coercively, or under conditions in which individuals are “offered” the use of these technologies in ways that are coercive, or under the guise of moral-enhancement, or similar.

passages.section: A. Application in the context of Law Enforcement
passages.text: As the UN Human Rights Council Advisory Committee has highlighted, the potential for the discriminatory use of neurotechnologies – particularly in relation to groups that have been marginalized, subjected to structural discrimination, or are socioeconomically disadvantaged – is a key concern. As with other technologies that have applications in these settings, including surveillance tools and artificial intelligence,neurotechnologies could likewise exacerbate existing discrimination and facilitate further abuses in the absence of strong oversight.

passages.section: A. Application in the context of Law Enforcement
passages.text: Finally, practical obstacles remain. Many of the technologies under consideration have not been tested for accuracy, reliability, or safety in real-world law enforcement environments. Without assessing privacy risks and consent issues as well as other human rights challenges, there cannot be public trust in new uses. Operational experiences to date have exposed critical regulatory gaps, underlining the need for clear governance frameworks that align innovation with human rights protection as established in human rights treaties and as interpreted by treaty monitoring bodies.

passages.section: B. Implications for the Criminal Justice System
passages.text: The use of neurotechnologies in investigations and the reliability and admissibility of neural data in court raise important concerns, particularly in criminal cases. For example, questions remain about the accuracy of technologies that seek to detect memory or deception. While there is no standardized approach to this globally, courts in some jurisdictions have assessed the admissibility of neuroimaging evidence on a case-by-case basis, determining the appropriate conditions under which it can be used. Additionally, the transnational flow of digital data raises complex cross-border challenges, as differences in national legal frameworks, enforcement capabilities, and regulatory maturity can hinder coordinated responses and accountability. More broadly, these are global questions that require global discussions.

passages.section: B. Implications for the Criminal Justice System
passages.text: Emerging examples of the use of neurotechnologies in the criminal justice system present questions around the lack of regulation and oversight. Should there be laws that restrict the use of neurotechnology in criminal investigations? Can courts legally order a criminal defendant, even in narrow circumstances, to cooperate with law enforcement in the use of neurotechnologies? Should neurotechnologies be used to support the social reintegration of formerly incarcerated individuals? How should these technologies be governed to prevent misuse, abuse, or discrimination in such high-risk contexts?

Finally, the emergence of neurotechnology also brings a host of evolving threats regarding potential malicious or criminal misuse. Unauthorized access to BCIs, manipulation of neural data, or the use of neurotechnologies for covert communication could present new and unprecedented threats to individual autonomy and societal security. Organized criminal groups could exploit these capabilities to plan and execute complex crimes faster than law enforcement can detect, disrupt, or investigate them.

Preventing, countering, and effectively responding to these threats therefore necessitates the development of specialized and constant training, field response protocols, and clear procedures for maintaining the chain of custody when handling neurotechnology-related evidence. These possible criminal misuses highlight why law enforcement, and the criminal justice system must stay ahead in understanding and regulating neurotechnology carefully.

Given the risks outlined above, it is imperative that the development and application of neurotechnologies in law enforcement and criminal justice be guided by robust safeguards that place human rights at the centre. Responsible use must begin with a solid, scientific, and technical foundation. Ensuring that these technologies are lawfully deployed requires a rigorous assessment of their impact on human rights.Technologies should therefore not be deployed until their accuracy, safety, and feasibility have been rigorously demonstrated through independent testing and peer-reviewed research. Policymakers, investigators, and courts must be equipped with clear and reliable information about what these tools can - and cannot - do, so that decisions are informed by sound evidence rather than speculation or overstatement.

It is furthermore of particular importance that there is clear communication about the implications of this evidence for settings outside the scientific and medical fields. To ensure the responsible use of neurotechnology in those cases, key precautionary measures must be implemented, including, but not limited to, establishing clear legal and ethical frameworks to protect human rights, ensuring voluntary and informed consent from individuals, implementing robust data protection and cybersecurity measures, and maintaining independent oversight to ensure accountability and address misuse.

Respect for human rights must remain paramount. Individuals must retain control over their neural data, and any interference with mental integrity or cognitive processes must be strictly limited, lawful, and subject to judicial oversight. Consent must be voluntary and informed, free of coercion or undue influence, particularly in custodial or correctional settings where power imbalances are acute. Safeguards must also ensure that neurotechnologies are not deployed in ways that reinforce existing inequalities or result in discriminatory impacts on marginalized groups.

Legal and ethical frameworks will need to evolve to provide clarity about permissible and impermissible uses of neurotechnology in both investigative and judicial contexts. This includes developing clear rules on admissibility of evidence, establishing independent mechanisms for oversight and accountability, and ensuring that any deployment is subject to transparency and democratic scrutiny. The creation of such frameworks should draw on expertise from multiple disciplines, including neuroscience, law, ethics, and human rights, to ensure that they are both scientifically robust and normatively sound.

Finally, the governance of neurotechnologies must be proactive and collaborative. Independent oversight bodies will be necessary to monitor applications and ensure compliance with human rights standards. Strong protections for data security and cybersecurity must be established to prevent unauthorized access to neural data. Because many of the challenges posed by neurotechnologies are transnational, international cooperation and harmonization of standards will be essential to addressing regulatory gaps and ensuring accountability across borders. Above all, transparency and inclusive dialogue will be necessary to build public trust, without which the use of these powerful technologies in justice and security settings would lack legitimacy.

Building on this background paper, a Technology Assessment will be developed to provide more comprehensive guidance on the actual or potential use, benefits, threats and risks of neurotechnologies in law enforcement and criminal justice systems. With that in mind, UNODC and INTERPOL are seeking insights from a broad range of stakeholders to inform this initiative. This public consultation aims to identify both the opportunities and risks associated with these emerging technologies, to ensure that any potential application in law enforcement and criminal justice upholds human rights, legal safeguards, and ethical principles.
UNODC and INTERPOL invite submissions that address considerations relevant to the use of neurotechnology under the umbrella of the intersection of neuroscience, law enforcement, and criminal justice.

passages.section: Neurotechnology and the Administration of Justice
passages.text: Submitted by: Futures Lab for Democracy, Tech & Human Rights, American University Contributors: Professor Jonathan Crock, Joy Adjei, Melodie Aygoren, Khaliun Batkhuyag, Will Bird, Shaima Caleb, Mariama Cham, Grace DePanise, Lily Diaz, Faith Forman, Micah Hinnergardt, Taekyung Hwang, Kenechukwu Ikeh, Jeeyoung Lee, Rocky Mamea, Sierra Mari, Savana Mullen, Sydney Ryan, Haewon Seo, Natalie Smith, and Lan Tran.

The rapid advancement of neurotechnology, particularly brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), presents transformative opportunities alongside human rights challenges. In 2024, the United States’ BRAIN Initiative achieved significant breakthroughs, including high-accuracy decoding of internal speech and advanced brain mapping. Private sector innovation has accelerated in parallel. Companies such as Neuralink and China’s NeuroXess are advancing implantable BCIs that translate neural signals into language and movement, while new chip technologies promise scalable commercialization. Although these developments are framed as life-changing tools for individuals with paralysis or neurological conditions, they remain in clinical stages and lack clear pricing structures, raising concerns about accessibility, equity, and long-term oversight.

Governance frameworks have not kept pace with innovation. Regulatory authority is fragmented across jurisdictions, and decision-making processes often privilege scientific, corporate, and state actors while marginalizing those most affected: patients, defendants, prisoners, and vulnerable communities. Uneven participation reinforces structural inequality. Human Rights Impact Assessments (HRIAs) are increasingly recognized as essential ex-ante safeguards, ensuring risks to privacy, autonomy, and mental integrity are evaluated before deployment. The case of Girardi v. Emotiv Inc., in which Chile’s supreme court ordered the deletion of neural data and suspended sales pending public health certification, demonstrates that commercialization cannot rely solely on click-through consent.

Legal protections vary widely. Within the United States, states such as California and Colorado have amended privacy laws to include neural data, yet no federal standard exists. By contrast, the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation and Artificial Intelligence Act embed human dignity and data protection into binding supranational law. Globally, there remains no unified international framework for neurorights, despite early leadership from countries such as Chile and guidance from organizations such as UNESCO and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Emerging neurotechnologies also amplify risks of discrimination. Biased datasets and predictive systems may disproportionately harm people of African descent, queer individuals, and other marginalized groups, particularly in policing, employment, and judicial contexts. The potential for cognitive surveillance, involuntary inference of identity traits, and unequal access to benefits underscores the urgency of enforceable safeguards.

Given these developments, the United Nations should establish global standards grounded in human dignity, cognitive liberty, and equality. Proactive oversight, independent audits, clear consent limitations, and meaningful participation of impacted communities are critical to ensuring neurotechnology advances justice rather than undermining fundamental human rights.

passages.section: 2. Latest Developments in Neurotechnology and Justice
passages.text: In 2024, the United States’ BRAIN initiative made notable developments in various fields, using BCI (Brain Computer Interface) to translate internal speech with 79 percent accuracy onto a monitor, publish the highest-to-date 3D resolution map of the human brain tissue, and workshop the Clinical Outcome Assessments with the Food and Drug Administration. But in 2025, the BRAIN initiative budget dropped by $81 million from the previous year due to congressional decreases of the 21st Cures Act funding, creating a slight worry for the future of BRAIN after their FY2026 budget expires.

passages.section: 2. Latest Developments in Neurotechnology and Justice
passages.text: Other notable advances include Elon Musk’s Neuralink: Telepathy, which allows the user to control a computer interface with their thoughts. Currently, it maintains 21 clinical patients worldwide.

passages.section: 2. Latest Developments in Neurotechnology and Justice
passages.text: To rival Neuralink, the Chinese NeuroXess has made a breakthrough as the world’s first to simultaneously decode language and movement in real time in a 21-year-old patient with epilepsy. Additionally, there are reports of a new silicone chip, much smaller and more efficient for brain computer interface, under development by Kampto Neurotech in the United States for commercial versions before preclinical research applications.

passages.section: 2. Latest Developments in Neurotechnology and Justice
passages.text: All these neurotechnological improvements are advertised as aids to people with severe physical and neurologic disabilities. However, there are major concerns surrounding the accessibility of these services and the lack of legal regulations.

In governance of neurotechnology in the administration of justice, decision-making powers are fragmented. Regulatory discussions involve diverse stakeholders, including scientists, businesses, human rights experts, and policymakers who often have different vocabularies, worldviews, and standards of success. The lack of explicit consensus across regulation strategies and disparate regulation recommendations have led to confusion and uneven compliance. This process fails to meaningfully engage citizens, marginalizing those most impacted. Failure of inclusion violates human rights and procedural justice while entrenching institutional and private interests, risking neurotechnology advancing as a product for market expansion while disregarding the human costs.

France’s Civil Code exemplifies this paradigm. France was the first country to allow brain imaging in judicial proceedings with consent, for medical or scientific research, or for forensic expertise, except for functional brain imaging. This policy was adopted prior to consensus among neuroscience experts and in opposition to the recommendations of the French Parliamentary Office for the Evaluation of Scientific and Technological Choices. Critics argue there is a lack of distinction among imaging types and unclear limits on use. These critiques illustrate the uneven participation and lack of consultation in a top-down, non-consultative lawmaking process.

Those directly impacted by neurotechnology, including defendants and prisoners, patients and users, vulnerable groups, and marginalized communities, are regarded as secondary advisors or “objects” in the regulatory process. At the global level, perspectives from low- and middleincome countries and the Global South are underrepresented. The human right to citizen participation, with respect to those most directly impacted, requires that citizens be given decision-making powers. The demand for independent audits and evaluations, establishment of redlines, and binding recommendations to enforcement agencies is critical to prevent regulatory capture. While there is promise in neurotechnology’s assistance in assessing guilt, accountability, and the risk of recidivism in judicial proceedings, it also carries risks regarding access to the regulatory process.

In the United States, some states have worked towards creating protections for neural privacy. California and Colorado are currently the only states to have passed legislation on neural data privacy, while a dozen others have legislation pending.

The California law grants consumers privacy rights regarding personal information and neural data. In this law, neural data is defined as “information that is generated by measuring the activity of a consumer’s central or peripheral nervous system, and that is not inferred from nonneural information.” The Colorado Privacy Act regulates “biological, genetic, biochemical, physiological, or neural properties, compositions, or activities or of an individual’s body or bodily function” as sensitive data that is to be protected from business use. California and Colorado demonstrate that there is no national standard on which biological data qualifies for privacy protections.

The European Union offers protection for the processing of neural and biometric data through guarantees of fundamental rights, data-protection laws, and criminal-procedure safeguards. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), established in 2018, ensures that personal and sensitive neurobiometric data about health and mental status are legally classified and protected. Only under specifications such as legal necessity, proportionality, and security may courts request the processing of said data. However, there is no international standard for the protection of neural and biometric data, and governments are insufficiently regulating new and emerging technologies. While general data privacy frameworks may provide some protections, specific international standards must be established to recognize the highly sensitive and personal nature of bio- and neurotechnologies.

passages.section: 5. Human Rights Risks and Needed Safeguards
passages.text: In the implementation of neurotechnology in the administration of justice, there is a critical need to assess risks and implement safeguards. Although UNESCO’s Universal Declaration on Bioethics and Human Rights in Article 6 mandates that “all scientific and medical interventions must be carried out with the individual’s prior, free, and informed consent,” neurotechnology has the capacity to violate personal sovereignty over one’s brain in ways that challenge traditional notions of autonomy, privacy, and personal identity.

passages.section: 5. Human Rights Risks and Needed Safeguards
passages.text: Neurorights safeguard fundamental aspects of human dignity, ensuring that mental processes and cognitive functions remain inviolable. They align with Articles 12 and 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) which protect privacy and freedom of thought, conscience, and religion. a. While the first international neurotechnological standard was set in 2019 by the Council of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), stricter legal protections must be enacted to protect the human right to sovereignty over one’s brain; secure the human right to participation in decision-making; and ensure free, prior, and informed consent. b. Second, independent regulatory bodies should transition from reactive enforcement to proactive regulation by evaluating “neurotechnology patents for potential social harms at the time of examination, and either directly notify relevant regulatory agencies or make evaluation results broadly available at the time of publication for granted patents.” c. Finally, technical safeguards such as encryption and privacy-preserving design should be mandated to prevent unauthorized access or manipulation. These safeguards ensure that neurotechnology serves justice without eroding human dignity or fundamental freedoms.

Human rights protections are facing technological, legal, and social threats that lead to discrimination and undermine equity and equality. Draft global standards on the ethics of neurotechnology underline that technologies must be developed and used in ways that avoid segregation, discrimination, or subordination of peoples, and promote gender-inclusive participation and representation throughout research and innovation. The UNESCO draft calls for gender-responsive policies to close gaps in access and leadership in neurotechnology, highlighting the importance of inclusive governance in emerging scientific fields. This reflects a broader shift in human rights approaches, in which participation, representation, and transparency are seen as essential safeguards against discrimination, rather than as optional policy goals.

Within the United States, the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division has articulated a commitment to confronting discrimination in emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, acknowledging the risk that AI systems may produce biased outcomes. These concerns are especially relevant for racial and gender equity, since algorithmic systems can often reproduce historical biases present in data or institutional practices. Ethical frameworks such as the Belmont Report further emphasize justice and equitable treatment in research contexts by ensuring fair distribution of benefits and preventing exploitation of vulnerable groups. Although developed for research on human subjects, its principles continue to guide contemporary discussions on fairness, accountability, and protection of vulnerable populations in technological development.

Taken together, these developments reflect evolving efforts to integrate gender equity and racial non-discrimination into human rights protections in law, policy, and technological governance. As innovation advances, maintaining human rights protections will depend on ensuring that technological systems are designed and governed to prevent discrimination and promote inclusion.

Human Rights Impact Assessments (HRIAs) are an ex-ante human rights due-diligence tool. They assess affected rightsholders and foreseeable risks before a technology is designed and deployed, and they require those findings to be reflected in design choices, data governance, and operational standards. In neurotechnology, this early timing matters because once neural data are collected, their use can readily expand through storage, analysis, inference, and reuse, and the resulting impacts on privacy, autonomy, and mental integrity are difficult to reverse. UNICEF cautions that in data-rich ecosystems, neurotechnology may threaten rights such as privacy and freedom of thought, and that wearable devices can enter the market without sufficiently rigorous oversight. The 2019 controversy over EEG headbands in a Chinese primary school, which led local education authorities to suspend their use, suggests how neurotechnology can slip into everyday settings faster than safeguards when no independently verifiable prior assessment is in place.

While the importance of HRIAs has gained attention, actual cases of corporate implementation and public disclosure remain limited. A representative case is Girardi v. Emotiv Inc. Senator Guido Girardi Lavin purchased a device from U.S.-based company Emotiv and later found that the terms of service restricted non-subscribers’ access to their neural data. The Chilean Supreme Court ruled that Emotiv had sold the device without adequate oversight of health and human rights, ordering the deletion of collected neural data and the suspension of sales until public health certification is obtained. This case showed that commercialization cannot be justified solely by click-through consent and emphasizes the need to institutionalize HRIAs as a pre-market requirement to protect privacy, mental integrity, and cognitive freedom.

As neurotechnology enters healthcare and legal fields, it exacerbates existing inequalities for marginalized communities, including for people of African descent and members of the LGBTQI+ community, through surveillance, biases, and weak accountability.

The human rights risks presented by neurotechnology can fall disproportionately on people of African descent and other marginalized communities who are underrepresented in neurotechnology datasets and decision-making power structures. The training data for these algorithms is often not diverse and draws on historical records, making outputs less accurate and potentially harmful to people of African descent and other marginalized communities.

There are also growing concerns about how neurotechnology may be used by institutions and governments. Since neurotechnology can affect cognition and emotion, its use in policing could expand into brain-reading of suspects or witnesses. Error-prone identification and biased prediction tools can also increase surveillance, arrests, and charging decisions that disproportionately affect people of African descent and other marginalized communities.

Neurotechnologies, such as brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), neural decoding systems, and affect recognition tools, also pose disproportionate risks to marginalized communities, particularly LGBTQI+ individuals, by intensifying surveillance and threatening cognitive privacy. Emerging “mind-reading” tools, for example, may infer sexual orientation or gender identity based on neural responses to stimuli, raising the possibility of involuntary outing in workplaces, medical contexts, or legal systems.

Existing research also shows that neurotechnology datasets often lack representative diversity, resulting in algorithmic biases that disproportionately harm marginalized populations. When LGBTQI+ individuals are underrepresented or misrepresented in neural datasets, neurotechnologies may produce inaccurate or pathologizing interpretations of their mental states. This mirrors broader patterns of technological bias in health and digital surveillance systems affecting LGBTQI+ communities. Robust regulatory safeguards and redistribution of decision-making power over neurotechnologies are required to prevent new forms of cognitive surveillance and discrimination and the acceleration of structural inequalities.

As we enter a new era of rapidly advancing neurotechnology and related innovations, the mechanisms for ensuring accountability and providing remedies when these technologies are misused in civil or criminal justice settings remain profoundly underexamined.

Given this, the United Nations needs to develop new human rights standards that reflect the emerging and rapidly evolving nature of neurotechnology. Until such standards are established, the use of neurotechnology, particularly in legal responses to violations of neurorights, should be subject to careful monitoring.

In the United States, the lack of national legislation on the development of neurotechnology is resulting in individual states taking piecemeal actions to regulate neurotechnology. States such as California and Colorado have revised their existing privacy laws and added neural data protections into their legislation. However, greater collaboration with stakeholders and examination of what neural data protection means to different stakeholders is needed to inform policies and expand laws to cover grey areas.

To begin addressing this issue, permissions should be clearly articulated when individuals are granted access to neurotechnology. Although this does not guarantee that their rights will be fully protected, ensuring users know what permissions they are granting is vital. At the same time, these permissions should be limited in scope. Individuals should not be able to consent to overly broad uses of neurotechnology until clear and established neurorights are in place.
